Launch Planning

Launch Narrative

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Understand the four categories of demo automation tools
  • Distinguish proof of capability (agent's job) from proof of experience (demo's job)
  • Structure demos as transformation narratives, not feature tours
  • Scale personalized demos with agent augmentation

The Demo Problem

Have you ever delivered a product demo? Stood in front of a Zoom screen, mid-sentence, the prospect leaning forward, and silently prayed to whatever deity governs staging environments?

Demos: High Stakes, Primitive Infrastructure

A great demo closes deals. A broken demo can kill months of pipeline development in ninety seconds. And yet most enterprise companies run demos on shared staging environments that are one bad deployment away from embarrassment. The "demo script" is usually a Google Doc that gets updated when someone remembers.

The agentic era is accelerating the transformation from demos-as-live-performance to demos-as-interactive-experience — and that changes the PMM's role entirely.

The Demo Landscape: Four Categories

1. Demo Environment Platforms

Sandboxed, customizable versions of your actual product. Functional replicas with realistic data you control, decoupled from production.

Examples: Demostack, Reprise

2. Interactive Demo Builders

Guided, self-serve product tours. Clickable walkthroughs with annotations, tooltips, branching paths. Lighter-weight than full environments.

Examples: Navattic, Supademo, Arcade

3. Demo Overlay Tools

Overlay customized data and narratives onto your actual product interface. Control what data appears without building a separate environment.

Examples: Saleo, Walnut

4. Asynchronous Demo Platforms

Personalized video demos buyers watch on their own. Track engagement at individual level — which features they spend time on, who else watched.

Examples: Consensus

What Is the Demo For?

If an AI agent can evaluate your product's technical capabilities from documentation, API specs, and architecture diagrams — what is the demo actually for?

Proof of Capability

  • Does the product do what marketing claims?
  • Technical verification of features
  • Integration compatibility
  • Being absorbed by agents

Proof of Experience

  • What does it feel like to use this?
  • Emotional connection to the transformation
  • Storytelling, not specification
  • The demo's primary job now

The Agent Knows Before You Demo

The prospect's agent already knows whether your product supports real-time data synchronization with SAP S/4HANA before the sales call starts. It read your API docs. What the agent can't do is make the prospect want the product. That's the demo's job — and that's a storytelling problem, not a technical problem.

Demo as Narrative

The best demo we've ever watched wasn't a feature walkthrough. It was a transformation story:

Step 1: Current State Pain

"Right now, your supply chain team gets a forecast update every Monday morning. They download a spreadsheet, manually reconcile it against the ERP data, and by Wednesday they have a planning view that's already two days stale."

Step 2: Transformation Moment

"Here's what Monday morning looks like with our platform..."

Step 3: Future State Resolution

"The forecast is live. The reconciliation is automatic. And your supply chain team spends Wednesday on strategy instead of spreadsheets."

The prospect didn't just see what the product did. They felt what their life would be like using it.

That's the demo that matters in the agentic era — the one that creates an emotional and experiential connection that no agent evaluation can replicate.

Personalizing Demos at Scale

The challenge with "demo as narrative" is that personalization doesn't scale in a traditional workflow. Building a customized narrative for every prospect — their industry, pain points, tech stack, organizational context — would consume a PMM's entire week.

💡 Agent Augmentation for Demo Prep

The same intelligence infrastructure that powers competitive enablement can power demo personalization:

  • Agent pulls prospect company data (industry, size, tech stack, recent news)
  • Combines with your use case library to generate customized demo script
  • PMM/SE reviews and adjusts — adds the specific anecdote, adjusts emphasis
  • Demo environment pre-configured with relevant data

Result: Personalized, narrative-driven demos prepared in hours instead of days.

The sales engineer's job shifts from building the demo to performing it — and performing it well is the part that actually wins deals.

The Practitioner's Playbook

1. Separate Capability from Experience

Make docs, API specs, and product pages detailed enough that an agent can evaluate technical capabilities without needing a live demo. This filters tire-kickers and saves everyone's time.

2. Invest in Demo Automation

Top-of-funnel: Interactive tour builders (Navattic, Supademo) — inexpensive, PMM can build.
Enterprise deals: Environment platforms (Demostack, Reprise) — eliminates staging crashes, enables deep personalization.

3. Build a Demo Narrative Library

Document 5-7 transformation stories that resonate. Before/after narratives with characters, tension, resolution. Agents can customize each for specific prospects; SEs have a foundation to build on.

Key Takeaways

  • Demo ROI is measured by absence: lost deals, wasted SE hours, broken staging environments
  • Proof of capability is being absorbed by agents — demos must focus on proof of experience
  • Demo as narrative: transformation stories, not feature tours
  • Four tool categories: Environment platforms, interactive builders, overlay tools, async platforms
  • Agent augmentation enables personalized demos at scale
  • Build a narrative library: 5-7 transformation stories agents can customize per prospect
